proposals.name: Mechanism named as a specific mathematical object
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract identifies the specific mathematical, physical, or structural object that does the work, rather than naming a pipeline of stages. 10: a concrete object is named and the abstract says which property of it produces the claimed effect (a stochastic Riemannian metric that characterizes a generator's distortion; a Cartesian-multipole anisotropic state that makes message passing directional; a finite-element discretization of an assumed PDE; a dot product of two vector fields with the role of each factor stated). 5: a mechanism is named but its link to the claimed effect is asserted, not explained. 0: the method is given only as a sequence of modules or as 'we combine A with B', so a reader cannot say which component carries the claim. Judge the text only; do not reward length.
proposals.rationale: R01, R23, R12 and R31 each hand the reader an object plus the reason it bites, and all sit in the dense_high_card_low half; a criterion bank scoring clarity, novelty and evaluation would see nothing special in them because they report modest or narrow experiments. The mirror cases are R05 and R51, which are card-favored and describe only an assembly (LoRA plus Gaussian kernels under homomorphic encryption; fuse the generative distributions of three LLMs) with no statement of which piece produces the gain.

proposals.name: Failure localized to a cause, then fix follows
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract localizes the failure it targets to a specific, checkable cause and then derives its remedy from that cause. 10: the cause is named concretely and the fix is its direct consequence (first-layer embedding gradients are much larger than the rest of the model, therefore freeze the embedding layer; clean and adversarial images behave as two domains, therefore estimate normalization statistics separately). 5: a plausible cause is offered but the proposed method does not obviously follow from it. 0: the deficiency is stated only in general terms ('existing methods struggle', 'a consistent gap is observed') and the remedy is a new architecture or objective with no stated causal link to the deficiency.
proposals.rationale: R49 and R44 are dense_high_card_low and are almost pure instances of diagnose-then-fix: both spend the abstract on the mechanism and propose an intervention that is one line long. R27 does the same for robustness (standard concentration ignores labels, so adapt the estimator to label uncertainty). Against these, card-favored R47 and R11 name a gap ('a consistent gap between full fine-tuning and quantization plus LoRA'; 'current methods struggle with rapid updates') and then introduce a framework whose connection to the gap is asserted rather than derived.

proposals.name: Subtractive contribution: something removed, fixed, or simplified
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the central claim is that something can be deleted, frozen, or reduced to a simpler form with little or no loss, and the abstract says what that implies. 10: the paper's headline is a removal or reduction and its consequence is stated (a diffusion model can be deconstructed until it is essentially a classical denoising autoencoder, and only a few components matter; the final classifier layer can be fixed up to a global scale with little accuracy loss, buying memory and speed). 5: a simplification is reported as one result among many. 0: the contribution is purely additive - more modules, more stages, more supervision - with no claim about what turns out to be unnecessary.
proposals.rationale: R33 and R48 are dense_high_card_low and both make removal the whole point; a scorecard rewarding methodological novelty and completeness will read them as thin, since neither introduces new machinery. R08 shows the same shape in a formal register (reframing learned Bloom filters as one optimization problem and getting near-optimal use of the existing model). The card-favored side, e.g. R11 and R16, is uniformly additive: new objective plus generated QA data plus target-model update; new representation plus learnable decoder plus UV sampling plus VAE plus latent diffusion.

proposals.name: Claim survives deletion of the proposed system
proposals.instruction: Ask what would remain if the authors' named artifact were deleted from the abstract. 10: at least one proposition about learning, data, or optimization remains that another researcher could carry away and test independently (a functional form that predicts generalization error across model and data scales; a characterization of when overfitting is benign, tempered, or catastrophic; an iteration complexity under a misaligned-gradient oracle). 5: a general claim is gestured at but is stated only as a property of the authors' system. 0: everything asserted is a property of the named system on named benchmarks, so deleting the system leaves nothing.
proposals.rationale: R54, R02 and R58 are dense_high_card_low and are almost entirely proposition rather than product, which also means they score poorly on the surface features a scorecard can check (no benchmark table, no released code, no ablation). The card-favored R50, R60 and R13 are the opposite: remove ProactiveBench, WizardMath or the personality-neuron pipeline and no transferable statement is left, yet each abstract is complete, quantified and well organized.

proposals.name: States conditions under which the claim holds
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the abstract bounds its own claim: assumptions, regime of validity, and approximation status. 10: the limits are stated in the authors' own voice ('under mild conditions'; 'we give rigorous analysis in a large local region'; 'using recently derived (non-rigorous) risk estimates under a Gaussian universality ansatz'), so a reader can say where the result would stop holding. 5: some scoping language appears but the operative claim is still unconditional. 0: claims are unconditional and intensified, with no regime, no assumption, and no acknowledgement that any condition is needed.
proposals.rationale: R02 flags its own non-rigor and its ansatz, R55 restricts its rigorous analysis to a local region, and R01 says 'under mild conditions' - all dense_high_card_low, and all penalized by the same honesty if a criterion bank credits confident, complete claims. In the card-favored direction, R11 promises 'near-optimal efficacy and long-term retention' and R60 reports 'extraordinary capabilities' with no stated condition anywhere.

proposals.name: Low density of promotional language
proposals.instruction: Score the abstract's language, not its content, for self-assessment and intensifiers. 10: the case is made in declarative statements, with essentially no words whose job is to tell the reader the work is good ('remarkable', 'striking', 'extraordinary', 'comprehensive', 'extensive', 'significantly', 'novel' used repeatedly, 'we reveal the extraordinary'). 5: a few intensifiers, mostly attached to specific measured quantities. 0: saturated with self-praise and superlatives, including praise of the paper's own results and of the field's importance. A plain abstract with weak content still scores high here; this criterion measures register only.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R58 are dense_high_card_low and are written flat, with no self-assessment at all, while card-favored R60 and R11 are dense in intensifiers ('remarkable', 'extraordinary', 'Remarkably', 'significantly outperforms', 'near-optimal'). R32 shows the same register in benchmark form ('comprehensive', 'carefully curated', 'widespread attention'). Intensifier density is exactly the kind of surface signal an explicit criterion bank tends to reward as confidence or impact, and that a text-level reader learns to discount.

proposals.name: Enumerated contributions are genuinely separable findings
proposals.instruction: Where the abstract enumerates contributions, score whether the items are independent findings or objects that could each stand without the others. 10: the enumerated items are separable - for instance two unrelated properties of the same training regime, one about normalization and one about network capacity, either of which could be published alone. 5: items are distinct but only as parts of one contribution. 0: the enumeration is the step list of a single pipeline (build a dataset, then use it to identify something, then use that to do a thing) or one idea partitioned into several labelled sub-claims. Abstracts that do not enumerate should be scored on whether their claims are separable in the same sense.
proposals.rationale: R44 enumerates two genuinely independent findings and R45 reports several distinct measurements of the early training phase; both are dense_high_card_low. Card-favored R13 ('three major technical contributions') and R19 (five named preference aspects) present one pipeline and one taxonomy respectively, cut into numbered pieces - a shape that reads as rich contribution to a bank counting contributions, and as one idea to a reader tracking what is actually separable. R11 uses bold headers for the same effect.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive result reported together with its explanation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract reports something a competent reader would not have predicted from the setup AND offers a mechanism for it. 10: both halves present (removing clean images from adversarial training raises robustness by 18.3%, explained by a two-domain hypothesis that then predicts the separate-normalization fix; networks are not robust to sign-preserving reinitialization, yet blurred-input pretraining approximates the same changes, suggesting they are label-agnostic). 5: a surprising result with no explanation, or a well-explained but wholly expected result. 0: every result runs in the direction the setup implies (a regularizer targeting quantization noise improves quantization robustness).
proposals.rationale: R44 and R45 are dense_high_card_low and both pair surprise with mechanism. Card-favored R29 and R47 report exactly what their own construction predicts - regularizing the first-order term improves robustness to that perturbation; a quantization-aware initialization narrows the quantization gap - which is legitimate and well written, and is the kind of tidy claim-to-evidence match an explicit bank scores highly while a reader registers no update.

proposals.name: Composition names the obstacle that made it hard
proposals.instruction: For abstracts that join two existing lines of work, score whether the obstacle to joining them is named and its resolution stated. 10: the blocker is precise and the fix answers it directly (applying the Winograd transform fills in exactly the sparsity that pruning creates, so move the ReLU into the Winograd domain and prune there; model-based offline RL compounds estimation error, so trade model-based against model-free estimates by their epistemic uncertainty and take a lower bound). 5: an obstacle is alluded to generically ('computationally intensive', 'architectures vary'). 0: the abstract states that two known techniques were used together and that the result is fast or accurate, without ever saying what was hard about the combination.
proposals.rationale: Card-favored R37 (ensemble Kalman filtering plus Gaussian belief propagation), R05 (LoRA plus Gaussian kernels plus homomorphic encryption) and R51 (fuse three pretrained LLMs) all present combinations as unproblematic and are rewarded for the tidy motivation-gap-method-results arc; R25 in the dense_high_card_low half names its obstacle and builds the method out of it. R42 shows the criterion cuts within a stratum rather than tracking it: it is card-favored yet names its obstacle sharply, which is the right behavior for a criterion that is meant to be a property of the text, not a proxy for the split.

proposals.name: Resource papers report a finding, not only scale
proposals.instruction: For abstracts introducing a benchmark, dataset, or evaluation metric, score whether a substantive thing learned from applying the resource is stated. 10: a specific finding about the systems evaluated, with direction and condition (a metric is shown robust to rephrasing and elongation that inflate a competing examiner; superimposed words distort classification but the distortion does not depend on the semantic relationship, so the word representation is not shared with the image representation). 5: a finding is claimed but stated only as 'reveals limitations' plus a headline number. 0: the abstract reports the artifact's size, modality coverage, curation effort and the number of models run, and summarizes outcomes as potential and limitations without saying what breaks or why.
proposals.rationale: R32 and R50 are card-favored and are almost entirely scale and process - 18K questions across 26 subcategories, 22 open-source and 6 closed-source models; 6,790 events, a reward model, an F1 of 66.47% - with the substantive result compressed to 'revealing some limitations'. R13 does the same for PERSONALITYBENCH. R57 and R46, in the other direction, each state a specific property that was learned by using the instrument. Resource-scale sentences are highly legible to an explicit bank (they answer 'is the evaluation thorough?') and carry little information about what was found.

proposals.name: Headline number interpretable and anchored to stated setting
proposals.instruction: Score the principal quantitative claim for interpretability and anchoring. 10: the number carries units or a directly meaningful scale and names the setting in which it was measured (time-of-flight error below 0.33 ns in indoor scenarios; the proportion of energetically favorable poses rises from 30% to 73% on a named docking benchmark). 5: a relative gain over a specific named baseline on a named benchmark. 0: a bare relative superlative over unnamed competitors ('surpasses all other open-source models by a substantial margin', 'significantly outperforms existing methods'), or a single score with no reference point.
proposals.rationale: R36 and R53 are dense_high_card_low and both report quantities a domain reader can convert into physical meaning without consulting a leaderboard. Card-favored R60, R11 and R50 report margins over unspecified fields or an isolated F1. A criterion bank asking 'are results quantified?' scores both kinds identically, since both contain numbers; the distinction between an anchored physical quantity and a free-floating margin is precisely what such a check cannot see.

proposals.name: Defines a new measurable quantity others could reuse
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract defines a quantity, ratio, or diagnostic that is separable from the paper's own method and could be measured by someone else on other systems. 10: the definition is explicit and portable (the cost of overfitting defined as the ratio of the interpolating model's test error to the optimally-tuned model's; label uncertainty of a region, used to re-derive an intrinsic robustness estimate; a mutual-information estimate between candidate and reference that needs no gold standard). 5: a quantity is introduced but is entangled with the authors' architecture. 0: only standard metrics are used and no new measurable is proposed.
proposals.rationale: R02, R27 and R57 are dense_high_card_low and each leave behind a definition rather than a system. A scorecard evaluating method novelty and empirical strength has no natural slot for 'left a reusable measurable behind', and these abstracts are otherwise sparse on the checkable surface features. Card-favored R41 and R51 introduce no measurable at all and are scored on the strength of their reported comparisons.

proposals.name: Every sentence adds a commitment; terse but non-empty
proposals.instruction: Score information density jointly with technical commitment - both halves are required. 10: each sentence introduces a new commitment (a construction, a condition, a quantity, a consequence) rather than re-motivating; a three-sentence abstract that names a specific generalization of dot-product attention and states what it is a good inductive bias for scores high, as does a long abstract in which every sentence adds a distinct claim. 5: a clear core surrounded by two or three sentences of restated motivation. 0: several sentences restate the same motivation or the same trade-off in different words, or survey adjacent work before any commitment is made; a long abstract whose commitments would fit in two sentences scores low here regardless of how well written it is.
proposals.rationale: R24 is three sentences and makes an architectural commitment in each; R08 and R58 are similarly compressed. All three sit in dense_high_card_low, and all three are hard for a bank that checks for stated motivation, stated evaluation, stated significance - short abstracts simply fail those checks. In the other direction R07 restates its trade-off across many one-sentence lines, R03 spends most of its length on framing and the psychology analogy, and R19 enumerates before committing; each is card-favored and reads as long rather than dense.

proposals.name: Positions against a specific account and names its gap
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract engages a particular existing explanation, taxonomy, or standard practice and states exactly what it gets wrong - not merely that prior work is insufficient. 10: the target and the defect are both specific (standard concentration of measure fails to characterize intrinsic robustness because it ignores labels; an existing benign/tempered/catastrophic taxonomy needs refinement and the paper says along which axis; most modern diffusion components turn out to be nonessential for representation learning). 5: prior work is named but its defect is generic. 0: prior work is characterized only as costly, impractical, or limited, with no account of what it claims or why the claim fails.
proposals.rationale: R27, R02 and R33 are dense_high_card_low and each argues with a named position rather than a citation cloud. Card-favored R51 and R11 describe prior approaches only by cost and inconvenience ('significant costs', 'redundant capabilities', 'often struggle with rapid updates', 'increasing storage requirements'), which satisfies a 'motivates against prior work' check while conveying no disagreement a reader could adjudicate.

proposals.name: Names its own cost; no free-lunch framing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states what its proposal gives up, and against what. 10: an explicit trade is named as part of the contribution (a generalization that allows trading sample efficiency against approximation accuracy; a method that trades model-free against model-based estimates according to their uncertainties and is deliberately conservative as a result). 5: a limitation is acknowledged in passing but not tied to the method's design. 0: the method is presented as strictly dominant - no extra parameters while ensuring near-optimal efficacy and long-term retention, large speedups while maintaining comparable performance - with no cost stated anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R53 and R25 are dense_high_card_low and build the trade-off into the statement of the contribution. Card-favored R11 and R05 present dominance without cost ('requires no extra parameters while ensuring near-optimal efficacy and long-term retention'; 6.94x and 2.3x speedups 'while maintaining performance comparable to plaintext models'). Costless framing reads as strength to an explicit bank checking whether benefits are clearly claimed, and as an unexamined claim to a reader who knows every such method pays somewhere.

proposals.name: Abstract length and elaboration volume
proposals.instruction: Estimate on 0-10 how long and elaborated this abstract is, using only visible text volume: approximate word count, number of sentences, and how many distinct sub-points are spelled out. 0 = extremely terse (two or three sentences, under about 80 words); 5 = a single moderate paragraph of about 150-200 words; 10 = very long or multi-paragraph, about 300 words or more with many elaborated sub-points. Score extent only. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is efficient, or whether being long or short is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Text volume tracks the scorecard side of this slice. The two most compact items, R31 (two sentences) and R49 (four sentences), sit at card_pct .018 and .014 while ranking dense_pct .999 and .712; R26 and R36 are likewise compact at card_pct .021 and .219. The longest items, R41, R09 and R59, sit at card_pct .986, .991 and .940, and R03 at .822. A fixed bank of criteria has more surfaces to fire on when more sentences are present, so sheer word count can buy scorecard credit without any additional research content.

proposals.name: Artifact-release and availability boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the text is devoted to statements that code, data, weights, checkpoints, demos or project pages are or will be released or publicly available, including promissory forms such as 'we will release'. 0 = no availability statement anywhere; 5 = one short standard sentence; 10 = several such statements, or a prominent multi-clause release block. Score only the presence and prominence of availability language. Do NOT verify the claim, do NOT judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice, and do NOT judge reproducibility.
proposals.rationale: Release boilerplate is concentrated on one side of the disagreement: R06 ('Code is released on our project page', card .980), R13 (card .965), R19 ('Both datasets are publicly available', card .961), R14 (card .947), R47 (card .918), R56 (card .920), R57 (card .926), R59 (card .940) and R21 ('We will release our code', card .784) are all dense_low_card_high, while dense_high_card_low items such as R31, R26 and R42 carry none. The sentence is one clause of costless text and a promissory form costs nothing at all; it fingerprints a group with staff to package artifacts rather than saying anything about the findings. Marked mixed because groups that can package artifacts plausibly also do more careful work.
proposals.upstream_parent: engineering headcount and lab release norms

proposals.name: Identity-revealing URLs, handles and organisation-named hosts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text contains strings that could identify the producing person, group or organisation: personal handles or personal names inside a repository URL, lab or company project-page domains, an organisation name inside a repository path, named institutional hosts. 0 = no URLs, or only neutral ones with no identifying token; 5 = one URL containing a handle or lab name; 10 = several identity-bearing links, or an explicitly organisation-branded host or path. Score only how identity-revealing the visible strings are. Do NOT try to infer or state who the producers actually are, do NOT judge their standing, and do NOT judge whether including links is good.
proposals.rationale: De-anonymising strings cluster on the card-high side: R57 links a path containing an organisation name, google-research (card .926); R06 gives a lab project page, ali-design.github.io (card .980); R41 an organisation host, opendatalab.github.io (card .986); R45 a personal page, yanghtr.github.io (card .731); R56 a repository under a full personal name (card .920); R13 and R11 repositories under personal handles (card .965 and .869). Reputation is an unseen upstream factor that can only bias a text-only model through traces like these, which is what makes the visible trace, not the reputation, the scorable thing. Marked mixed because recognisable groups plausibly also produce stronger work. Note R17 carries a bare video link with no organisational token and sits at card .019, so a neutral URL is not the same feature.
proposals.upstream_parent: author or lab identity and reputation

proposals.name: Importance preamble before any contribution is stated
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the opening is spent asserting that the problem area matters before anything the work itself did is named. Look for constructions such as 'X is essential/critical/central', 'X is widely adopted in mission-critical applications', 'X raises serious concerns', and count how many sentences pass before the first sentence describing what was actually done. 0 = the first sentence already states what was done; 5 = one framing sentence of stakes; 10 = three or more sentences of stakes, motivation and concern before any contribution appears. Score only the amount of importance-framing. Do NOT judge whether the stated importance is true, and do NOT judge whether framing the stakes is good writing.
proposals.rationale: The stakes-first template sits on the card-high side: R13 opens 'Handling implicit language is essential...' (card .965), R56 'Efficient inference in high-dimensional models is a central challenge' (card .920), R34 'A critical component to enabling intelligent reasoning ... is memory' (card .813), R28 'critical to ensure their safety against adversarial attacks' (card .805), R30 'widely adopted in mission-critical applications' (card .786). The dense-favoured items instead open on the object itself: R26 'We study the cost of overfitting', R31 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer', R42 'We seek to uncover'. Stakes language is a rehearsable opening move, so any bank criterion resembling 'is the problem motivated' can be satisfied by writing habit alone. Marked mixed because groups that teach the template may also mentor better research.
proposals.upstream_parent: writing coaching and abstract templates taught inside the producing group

proposals.name: Residual markup and PDF-extraction artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the density of visible typesetting residue: TeX-style doubled-backtick or doubled-apostrophe quotes, backslash macros left unrendered (url, emph, escaped percent signs), an undefined macro name appearing as a bare word, stray brace characters inside a URL, markdown asterisk emphasis, and words split by a hyphen plus space where a line break was, such as 'fine- tuning'. 0 = clean prose with none; 5 = one or two such artifacts; 10 = many artifacts or a badly mangled span. Score only how much residue is visible. Do NOT judge whether it looks sloppy, careless or unprofessional, and do NOT infer anything about the care taken over the work.
proposals.rationale: Residue is unevenly distributed and is purely a property of the production and extraction pipeline, not of the research. R21 carries three broken-hyphenation splits, 'fine- tuning', 'discrep- ancy', 'lan- guage' (card .784); R15 carries 'sur- rounding' plus markdown bold (card .768); R56 has a stray brace pair inside its repository URL (card .920); R11 an unrendered url macro (card .869); R30 an unrendered emph macro (card .786). On the other side R04 leaks an undefined macro name straight into a sentence while sitting at dense 1.000 and card .095, so the artifact appears in both directions and is exactly the kind of orthographic regularity a text-only model can latch onto for no legitimate reason.

proposals.name: Enumerated contributions and typographic signposting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text is explicitly signposted as an enumerated list of contributions: phrases such as 'three major technical contributions', 'First/Second/Third', 'Firstly ... Finally', numbered items of the form (1) ... (2) ..., and bolded or otherwise emphasised key terms and system names. 0 = flowing prose with no enumeration and no emphasis; 5 = a single 'First ... Second' pair, or one emphasised term; 10 = a fully enumerated contribution list, or several emphasised terms together with numbered items. Score only the amount of enumeration and emphasis present. Do NOT judge whether the enumerated contributions are substantial, and do NOT judge whether the structure helps the reader.
proposals.rationale: Signposting concentrates on the card-high side: R23 announces 'three major technical contributions' then runs First/Second/Third (card .957); R15 numbers and bolds (1) Efficacy and (2) Retention plus its bolded system name (card .768); R59 bolds five named preference types (card .940); R09 runs Firstly/Then/Finally (card .991); R08 runs First/Second/Finally (card .960). A criterion such as 'are the contributions clear' can be answered by the presence of the enumeration itself, and the layout habit transfers to any content whatsoever. Marked mixed because the same mentoring that installs the template may accompany better work. Counter-instance: R50 also enumerates First/Second yet sits at card .039.

proposals.name: Natural-science and engineering application jargon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the density of specialist vocabulary drawn from an application discipline outside core machine learning: structural biology and chemistry (protein-ligand, docking, binding affinity, molecular motifs, side-chain angles, multipoles, QM/MM), physics and engineering (electromagnetic propagation, time-of-flight, antennas, finite element method, partial differential equations, sea surface temperature), clinical or sensor domains. 0 = entirely core-ML vocabulary; 5 = a handful of domain terms; 10 = the text is largely written in the target discipline's terminology. Score only how much such vocabulary appears. Do NOT judge whether the domain is important, whether the domain usage is correct, or whether interdisciplinary work is good.
proposals.rationale: Application-domain vocabulary sits almost entirely on the dense_high_card_low side: R05 (flow matching over protein-ligand data, card .339), R12 (docking, PDBBind, energetically favorable poses, card .126), R46 (Cartesian multipoles, QM/MM, fast multipole method, card .088), R48 (motif vocabulary, QED, SA, binding affinity, card .058), R53 (electromagnetic propagation, time-of-flight, antennas, card .136), R38 (finite element method, sea surface temperature, card .112). A criterion bank written in generic ML language has fewer hooks in this vocabulary, and which specialist versus generalist audience an item is routed to is an upstream process fact about the receiving side, not a property of the research.
proposals.upstream_parent: which reader pool and expertise the item is routed to on the receiving side

proposals.name: Counted experimental scale and named comparison systems
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much explicitly counted experimental scale is recited in the text: numbers of systems compared, named third-party or proprietary systems listed by name, dataset item counts, corpus sizes, numbers of benchmarks, tasks or subcategories. 0 = no counts and no named comparison systems; 5 = one dataset count, or a couple of named baselines; 10 = several counted quantities together with a roster of named systems. Score only how much counted scale is stated. Do NOT check whether the numbers are impressive, adequate or accurate, and do NOT judge the experiments themselves.
proposals.rationale: Recited scale clusters on the card-high side: R41 states 18K curated questions across 26 subcategories with 22 open-source and 6 closed-source systems evaluated (card .986); R09 states a 6,790-event generated dataset (card .991); R55 lists ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro and Mistral Medium as comparison points (card .883); R54 cites a memory of 150 million Wikipedia mentions (card .954); R25 names Llama-2, MPT and OpenLLaMA (card .765). Budget is an unseen upstream factor, and this recitation is its textual fingerprint: a bank criterion about experimental breadth converts spend directly into score. Marked mixed because resources plausibly buy both the recital and genuinely more thorough work, so it must also appear in the undiscounted band.
proposals.upstream_parent: compute, API and annotation budget available to the producer

proposals.name: Paid human-labour fingerprints: annotators, user studies, crowd platforms
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text reports work performed by recruited or paid humans: hired annotators labelling data, humans authoring or revising items, a user study, a crowd-platform evaluation, collected human preference data. 0 = no human labour mentioned at all; 5 = a single passing mention of human evaluation; 10 = human labour is described as a substantial component with its own procedure. Score only how much human-labour activity is described. Do NOT judge whether the human study was well designed, well powered or ethical, and do NOT judge whether human evaluation is preferable to automatic evaluation.
proposals.rationale: Every item in this slice that reports recruited human labour lands on the same side of the disagreement: R09 has human annotators labelling generated task predictions (card .991), R19 tasks humans with revising each document (card .961), R13 runs a user study against human evaluations (card .965), R57 reports a Mechanical Turk evaluation (card .926). No dense_high_card_low item reports paid human work. Being able to pay annotators is an upstream resource fact whose only textual trace is the mention itself, so a criterion rewarding human validation converts budget straight into score. Marked mixed because human validation can also reflect genuine methodological care.
proposals.upstream_parent: funding and institutional infrastructure for paid annotation

proposals.name: Contemporary large-language-model and agent subject-matter vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how saturated the text is with current large-language-model and agent vocabulary: large language models or LLMs, agents, prompts, instruction tuning, alignment or preference optimisation, LoRA, quantised serving of LLMs, multimodal LMMs, named recent chat systems. 0 = none of this vocabulary; 5 = the topic touches it in passing; 10 = the text sits entirely inside that vocabulary. Score only vocabulary saturation. Do NOT judge whether the topic is timely, important, fashionable, crowded or overdone.
proposals.rationale: This vocabulary is heavily on the card-high side: R09, R15, R21, R23, R25, R27, R41, R55 and R59 all carry it with card_pct running from .765 to .991, while the dense_high_card_low side is dominated by pre-LLM reinforcement-learning, optimisation and theory vocabulary (R17 card .019, R31 card .018, R42 card .025, R24 card .079, R32 card .138). Terminology vintage records when an item was produced, not what it is worth, and it can shift a text-only model wholesale. Counter-instances exist (R29, R34 and R07 use older vocabulary yet score card-high), which is why this is proposed as a suspected nuisance to be discounted rather than a confirmed effect.
proposals.upstream_parent: production and submission timing (topical cohort of the corpus)

proposals.name: Explains causal mechanism, not just that it works
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the abstract explains WHY the reported phenomenon/method works, not merely THAT it works. A 10 states a specific causal or mechanistic hypothesis (an underlying cause, a decomposition into contributing factors) and indicates it was tested or isolated. A 0 reports only that a method/finding holds (e.g., 'our method improves X by Y%') with zero explanation of the underlying cause.
proposals.rationale: R01 explains that early-training changes are 'label-agnostic' by showing blurred-input/self-supervised pretraining approximates them, and that labels merely accelerate the process; R28 proposes an explicit 'two-domain hypothesis' to explain why batch norm hurts adversarial robustness. Contrast R07 and R17, which report gains from neuron-editing / RLEIF pipelines with no causal account of why they work.

proposals.name: Reports a counterintuitive finding against plausible expectation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract reports a result that would surprise a knowledgeable reader relative to standard expectation, signaled explicitly or through contrastive phrasing ('despite', 'unexpected', 'intriguing', 'surprisingly'). A 10 clearly frames an unexpected/counterintuitive result and why it defies expectation. A 0 reports an expected, incremental improvement with no surprise framing.
proposals.rationale: R11 shows a classifier's entire final weight layer can be fixed with 'little or no loss of accuracy,' contradicting the assumption that this layer must be learned; R28 explicitly calls its results 'intriguing' and finds that removing clean training images boosts adversarial robustness. Contrast R39 and R17, which report large quantitative gains framed as straightforward wins rather than surprises.

proposals.name: Uses a minimal isolating construction vs stacked techniques
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the core contribution is demonstrated via a small, tightly controlled construction that isolates one phenomenon (10), versus a pipeline assembled from several distinct named sub-modules or techniques stacked together to produce the result (0).
proposals.rationale: R31 deliberately builds a 'minimalist example' to explain edge-of-stability training dynamics; R46 reduces learned Bloom filter design to a single clean optimization derivation. Contrast R41, which chains five categorized preference types through a multi-stage optimization pipeline, and R23 (SELF-PARAM), which combines a multi-part efficacy/retention framework with KL-based distillation.

proposals.name: Existence-only proof vs constructive, demonstrated theoretical claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on (a) whether the abstract makes a formal/theoretical claim AND (b) whether that claim is tied to an explicit construction, algorithm, or experiment that instantiates it. A 10 is a precise theoretical claim accompanied by a concrete algorithm, construction, or experiment demonstrating it in practice. A 0 is a purely existential claim ('there exists...', 'we prove the existence of...') with no accompanying construction, algorithm, or empirical demonstration reported in the abstract.
proposals.rationale: R19 proves only that certified-robust networks 'exist,' with no construction or experiment reported in the abstract; contrast R14, which derives an explicit optimization algorithm with stated iteration complexity and applies it to a concrete hidden-convexity problem, and R31, which builds and analyzes an explicit minimal function.

proposals.name: Ablation/diagnostic design vs leaderboard-only benchmark reporting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract signals a design that isolates individual causal factors (ablations, controlled comparisons of specific components, targeted diagnostic measurements) as opposed to reporting only aggregate end-task scores against baselines. A 10 names an explicit ablation/diagnostic study design. A 0 reports only final benchmark numbers versus baselines with no mention of isolating components.
proposals.rationale: R28 explicitly separates the roles of normalization and network capacity via targeted diagnostic experiments ('first rigorous study on diagnosing elements of...training'); R01 performs 'extensive measurements of the network state and its updates' to isolate specific early-training factors. Contrast R17 and R39, which report only benchmark score comparisons against named baselines.

proposals.name: Actionable recommendation that changes a widespread default practice
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract yields a concrete, generalizable recommendation that would change a widely-used default practice for many practitioners, stated with the conditions under which it applies. A 10 gives a specific 'do X instead of Y when Z' prescription targeting a near-universal component or practice. A 0 has a takeaway of 'our new artifact scores best,' with no transferable prescription for practice outside the paper's own system.
proposals.rationale: R33 gives a precise, conditioned prescription (freeze the embedding layer, then plain SGD beats AdamW) applicable to fine-tuning broadly; R11 recommends fixing the classifier layer, a near-universal network component. Contrast R02 and R17, whose payoff is a specific fine-tuned model/benchmark rather than a transferable practice change.

proposals.name: New unifying formalism vs spliced existing-technique combination
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the core contribution is a genuinely new unifying formalism or derivation (10), as opposed to an explicit splice of two or more pre-existing named techniques signaled by a compound description such as 'X-friendly/aware Y' or 'X applied to Y' (0).
proposals.rationale: R15 ('Encryption-Friendly LLM Architecture') explicitly splices homomorphic encryption + LoRA fine-tuning + Gaussian kernels; R10 (LoftQ) explicitly splices quantization with a LoRA initialization scheme. Contrast R05, which derives a new anisotropic multipole-based message-passing formalism, and R21, which derives its model directly from the finite element method applied to an unknown PDE.

proposals.name: Depth of non-LLM domain-specific scientific formalism used
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much domain-specific scientific or mathematical formalism (physics, chemistry, biology, control, optimization theory) the abstract requires and uses to state its contribution, independent of any LLM/NLP framing. A 10 states the contribution using nontrivial domain-specific structure (e.g., PDEs, multipole expansions, molecular geometry, robot dynamics). A 0 states the contribution purely in generic model-training/prompting/benchmarking vocabulary with no domain-specific formalism.
proposals.rationale: R05 builds on Cartesian multipole electrostatics for QM/MM systems; R21 derives its model from the finite element method applied to an unknown PDE governing sea-surface temperature and gas-flow dynamics. Contrast R02 and R07, whose formalism is entirely generic LLM-agent/fine-tuning vocabulary.

proposals.name: Specific technical problem framing vs generic trend-hype opening
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the opening motivation of the abstract: a 10 means the first 1-2 sentences state a precise technical gap or question specific to the problem; a 0 means the opening leans on a generic industry-trend claim ('X have shown remarkable Y', 'with the rapid development of Z') that could preface almost any paper in the area.
proposals.rationale: R02 opens with 'Agents powered by large language models have shown remarkable abilities in solving complex tasks'; R06 opens with 'With the rapid development of AI-generated content, the future internet may be inundated...'. Contrast R11 and R46, which open directly with the specific technical object under study.

proposals.name: Single throughline argument vs enumerated contribution checklist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 inversely with the presence of an explicit numbered list of separate contributions/technical pieces ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ...' or bolded parallel labels) used to describe the paper's approach. A 10 presents one continuous argument/method with no enumerated contribution list. A 0 explicitly enumerates three or more distinct technical contributions or components as a checklist.
proposals.rationale: R07 lists 'three major technical contributions' (a benchmark dataset, a neuron-identification method, and an induction method); R23 frames its method around two named enumerated factors ('Efficacy' and 'Retention') plus a multi-part pipeline. Contrast R46 and R53, each presented as one continuous throughline argument.

proposals.name: Superiority claims backed by explained mechanism or conditions
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether broad outperformance claims ('outperforms all X and Y models', 'surpasses...by a substantial margin') are accompanied by an explanation of the specific mechanism or condition responsible for the gain. A 10 means any superiority claim is tightly scoped and explained (why or when it wins). A 0 means sweeping outperform-everyone claims are made with no accompanying mechanistic or conditional explanation.
proposals.rationale: R02 claims to outperform 'all open-source and close-source models' with no explanation of why; R17 claims to surpass ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro, and Mistral Medium with no mechanistic account beyond naming the training recipe. Contrast R33, which explains precisely when and why SGD beats AdamW.

proposals.name: Low packaging density: few coined acronyms, sparse raw statistics
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 inversely with 'packaging density': count coined acronyms/brand names for the method, dataset, and/or benchmark together with the frequency of standalone specific numbers (percentages, counts, sample sizes) not woven into an explanatory sentence. A 10 uses plain descriptive language, at most one simple method name, and numbers only in service of a stated argument. A 0 uses multiple coined acronyms (e.g., separate names for the dataset and the benchmark) plus several free-standing statistics presented as a checklist of achievements.
proposals.rationale: R06 (LOKI) reports '18K carefully curated questions across 26 subcategories' and '22 open-source LMMs and 6 closed-source models' as a checklist of scale statistics; R23 coins SELF-PARAM as a nested acronym-of-an-acronym. Contrast R27 and R46, which use no coined branding and almost no free-standing statistics.

proposals.name: Portable general insight vs value tied to the specific artifact
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central claim would remain useful and informative to researchers who never adopt the specific artifact (model/dataset/benchmark) introduced, because it states a principle, characterization, or law about the broader problem space. A 10 is a portable characterization of a general phenomenon. A 0 is a finding whose value is entirely contingent on adopting the specific named system/dataset introduced.
proposals.rationale: R32 characterizes the functional form of generalization error 'across scales' as a general law usable independent of any specific model; R16 answers the general question of whether generative modeling of photos is a 'solved problem' and characterizes GAN limits broadly. Contrast R06 and R41, whose value is tied to adopting the specific named benchmark/system introduced.

proposals.name: Information-dense abstract with no repeated or filler framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on information density: a 10 means nearly every sentence introduces a new, distinct technical claim, with no repeated framing or generic filler sentences; a 0 means the abstract restates its motivation or importance multiple times in different words, or spends multiple sentences on generic context before any specific claim appears.
proposals.rationale: R27's three-sentence abstract states the architecture, the mechanism, and the application with no filler (dense_pct=0.999, the highest in the slice); contrast R06 and R41, which restate motivation across several sentences (R41 explains the general simultaneous-translation setup, then re-explains it as 'human preferences,' then re-explains it via five preference categories) before reaching the core contribution.

proposals.name: Positions against a fundamental question, not one prior paper
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract positions its contribution against a long-standing/fundamental open question in the field (10) versus as a targeted fix to a gap in one specific recently-cited prior method (0), evidenced by whether the abstract names its point of departure as a broad unresolved problem or as a single recent paper/technique.
proposals.rationale: R53 frames its question as understanding 'the cost of overfitting' as a basic phenomenon spanning benign/tempered/catastrophic regimes; R32 calls the dependency of generalization error on model/data scale a matter 'of critical importance both in practice and for understanding the theory of neural networks.' Contrast R10 (LoftQ), which frames its gap explicitly relative to 'Dettmers et al., 2023,' and R41 (SimulPL), framed as filling a gap in 'existing methods' for one specific pipeline stage.

proposals.name: Abstract length and sentence-count verbosity
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how long and elaborated the abstract is, based purely on word count, sentence count, and number of paragraph breaks -- NOT on what claims it makes or how good the work sounds. Score 0 if the abstract is extremely terse (roughly 1-3 short sentences), 5 for a typical single-paragraph abstract of moderate length, and 10 if it is unusually long and multi-paragraph with many clauses. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, well-used, or a sign of quality -- only report how much length/verbosity is present.
proposals.rationale: R13 ('Logic and the 2-Simplicial Transformer') is a two-sentence abstract yet has dense_pct=0.999 (top of dense) but card_pct=0.018 (near-bottom of scorecard); by contrast R34 and R45 are long, multi-clause, multi-paragraph abstracts with card_pct=0.920 and 0.986 respectively. Length is a pure textual surface feature that plausibly drives scorecard aggregation (more text = more surface for criteria to find something to reward) independent of the underlying research's merit.

proposals.name: Enumerated-list / bolded-keyword structuring
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract uses explicit enumeration markers (e.g. 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', '(1) ... (2) ... (3) ...') or bolded/emphasized key terms to lay out its claims, independent of the content of those claims. 0 = plain prose with no such markers; 10 = heavily itemized and/or bolded throughout. Do not judge whether the itemization makes the abstract clearer, more organized, or better -- only report how much of this formatting habit is present.
proposals.rationale: R16 bolds '**Efficacy**' and '**Retention**' and separately numbers them, and R23 bolds five named preference categories ('**translation quality preference**', etc.); both are dense_low_card_high with card_pct=0.768 and 0.940. This layout habit is a template/formatting choice, not evidence of research quality, but could make criteria easier for a scorecard judge to locate and check off.

proposals.name: Coined acronym/brand name in the title
proposals.instruction: Read the title and abstract. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the title coins and foregrounds an invented capitalized acronym or brand name for the proposed method (e.g., a memorable all-caps or CamelCase name standing in for 'our method'). 0 = purely descriptive title with no coined name; 10 = title is dominated by a prominent invented brand/acronym. Do not judge whether the name is a good name or whether branding indicates a better method -- only report how much brand-coinage is present.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('LoftQ'), R33 ('WizardMath'), R45 ('LOKI'), and R59 ('InfinityGAN') all coin a prominent brand name in the title and are in the dense_low_card_high subset (card_pct=0.784, 0.883, 0.986, 0.882); this naming convention is an orthographic/marketing habit, not a quality signal.

proposals.name: Public code/data release boilerplate statement
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the abstract contains a boilerplate statement announcing public release of code, data, or model weights (e.g. 'Our code is available at github.com/...', 'Code: url', 'will be released'). 0 = no such statement; 10 = an explicit, prominent release statement with a concrete link or clear promise. Do not judge whether releasing code is a good practice or reflects a better paper -- only report whether this boilerplate phrase is present.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('Our code, model weights, and data are public at ...') and R25 ('Our metric is publicly available at github.com/...') both carry this exact boilerplate and are dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.765 and 0.965); this is a template phrase tied to engineering/open-source norms rather than to the quality of the underlying research idea.

proposals.name: LLM/generative-AI topical vocabulary density
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the abstract uses large-language-model/generative-AI vocabulary (terms like 'LLM(s)', 'large language model', 'GPT', 'agent', 'prompt', 'fine-tuning', 'alignment', 'preference optimization'), regardless of the technical content behind those words. 0 = no such vocabulary (e.g., abstract is about classical ML/RL/optimization/theory topics); 10 = saturated with this vocabulary. Do not judge whether the topic choice is a good one or a trendy one -- only report the density of this specific vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('Proactive Agent...LLM agents...ProactiveBench') and R33 ('WizardMath...LLMs...mathematical reasoning') are saturated with this vocabulary and are dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.991, 0.883), while R10 ('kernel ridge regression'), R13 ('2-simplicial Transformer' for RL), and R35 ('generalization error across scales') use none of it and are dense_high_card_low. Topic-vocabulary choice is a subject-matter marker, not a quality signal.

proposals.name: Explicit comparison to named commercial frontier models
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract explicitly names specific commercial/proprietary frontier systems as baselines, tools, or comparison points (e.g. 'GPT-4', 'GPT-4o', 'ChatGPT', 'Claude', 'Gemini'). 0 = no such names; 10 = multiple such names are central to the comparison. Do not judge whether beating or using these systems indicates a better paper -- only report how much explicit name-dropping of branded commercial systems is present.
proposals.rationale: R33 explicitly beats 'ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro and Mistral Medium' and R23 uses 'GPT-4/4o' to generate its training data; both are dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.883, 0.940). Naming and comparing against costly proprietary frontier models requires both being active in the current hype window and having API budget -- an upstream resourcing/timing factor that could genuinely correlate with more thorough work (mixed) but is not itself research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing riding a topic-fashion wave, combined with access to proprietary-API compute budgets

proposals.name: Breadth of enumerated baselines/models/datasets compared
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how many distinct named baseline systems, models, or datasets the abstract explicitly enumerates as having been compared against or evaluated on. 0 = no baselines/datasets named; 10 = a long explicit list (many named systems/datasets). Do not judge whether the breadth of comparison makes the paper more rigorous or better -- only count/estimate how much enumerated breadth is present in the text.
proposals.rationale: R45 enumerates '22 open-source LMMs and 6 closed-source models' across '18K...questions across 26 subcategories' (card_pct=0.986) and R55 names 'MOPO', 'MOReL', 'COMBO' as baselines across '11 out of 18 benchmark datasets' (card_pct=0.324). Running such broad comparisons requires substantial compute/engineering resources upstream of any writing choice, and is plausibly rewarded by a criterion-based scorecard as 'thoroughness' independent of the core idea's merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional compute and engineering-team capacity to run large-scale evaluations

proposals.name: Decimal-precision numeric result reporting
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract reports its quantitative results with fine-grained decimal precision (e.g. '66.47%', '0.33ns', '116.4%') as opposed to round or qualitative claims. 0 = no numeric results or only round numbers; 10 = multiple decimal-precision figures. Do not judge whether the precision reflects rigor or a better result -- only report how much decimal-level numeric specificity is present.
proposals.rationale: R02 reports 'an F1-Score of 66.47%' and R05 reports '<0.33ns error in time-of-flight predictions'; producing and reporting results at this precision presupposes measurement infrastructure and repeated-trial budgets upstream of the writing itself, which is plausibly rewarded by a scorecard's 'rigor' criteria without being research quality per se.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional experimental infrastructure that enables fine-grained measurement and reporting

proposals.name: Confident, unhedged promotional framing
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how confident and unhedged the abstract's claims are -- i.e., the near-absence of hedging/caveat language ('may', 'preliminary', 'in some cases', 'a limitation is', 'future work should') combined with unqualified success claims ('significantly outperforms', 'achieves state-of-the-art'). 0 = heavily hedged, cautious, caveat-laden prose; 10 = fully confident, caveat-free, promotional prose throughout. Do not judge whether the confidence is warranted or whether the paper is actually good -- only report how confident/unhedged the tone is.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('significantly elicit the proactiveness...outperforming all open-source and close-source models') and R33 ('WizardMath 70B even outperforms ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro and Mistral Medium') read as fully confident, hedge-free promotional prose and are both dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.991, 0.883). Polished, unhedged framing is plausibly a product of editing support/experience rather than of the research itself, though genuinely stronger results might also license more confident language (hence mixed).
proposals.upstream_parent: professional editing or PR-style polishing of the abstract (e.g., by a senior co-author or communications-savvy team)

proposals.name: Canonical 'gap-then-solution' rhetorical template
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how closely the abstract follows the canonical three-move template: (i) state a widely-acknowledged limitation/gap in prior work, (ii) announce 'In this paper/work we propose/address...', (iii) close with a quantified success claim. 0 = abstract does not follow this template at all; 10 = abstract follows all three moves clearly and in this order. Do not judge whether following this template makes the abstract better-written or the work more compelling -- only report how closely this specific rhetorical formula is followed.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('Despite significant advancements in...LLMs, the rapid and frequent integration...remains a substantial challenge. ... In this paper, we propose...') and R52 ('...LLMs are expected to accurately output answers... In this work, we argue...') both execute this exact template and are dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.768, 0.967). This formulaic move is taught in writing workshops/mentorship rather than being evidence of the underlying idea's quality, though better-mentored authors might also produce genuinely stronger work (hence mixed).
proposals.upstream_parent: author exposure to formal scientific-writing mentorship/training conventions (a seniority- and institution-linked pedagogy effect)

proposals.name: Problem-Mechanism Alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed mechanism directly addresses a precisely diagnosed failure mode; score 0 when the method is only loosely connected to a broad problem statement.
proposals.rationale: R09, R17, and R27 connect specific failure mechanisms to targeted interventions, a relationship a text-sensitive model may perceive beyond generic method descriptions.

proposals.name: Falsifiable Conceptual Claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract advances a clear, non-obvious hypothesis that could distinguish competing explanations; score 0 when it offers only an untestable claim of improvement or novelty.
proposals.rationale: R18, R32, and R55 formulate precise explanatory or predictive claims rather than merely introducing systems, which may be underrepresented by checklist criteria.

proposals.name: Minimal Change, Broad Leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a small, clearly specified intervention produces broad conceptual or practical leverage; score 0 when the contribution depends on an unnecessarily elaborate collection of components.
proposals.rationale: R02, R23, and R44 each emphasize a focused change with substantial implications, a form of elegance that broad novelty or completeness criteria may miss.

proposals.name: Structure-Matched Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture encodes the problem’s relevant geometry, dependencies, hierarchy, or symmetry; score 0 when the architecture is generic and imposes no visibly relevant structural bias.
proposals.rationale: R12, R41, R57, and R59 build model structure around sensor dynamics, physical discretization, state-goal interactions, or higher-order logic.

proposals.name: Nuisance-Preserving Realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly accommodates difficult real-world conditions rather than removing them through convenient preprocessing or assumptions; score 0 when those conditions are ignored or idealized away.
proposals.rationale: R05, R12, R50, and R56 address black-box dynamics, irregular observations, conflicting data, or long-term partial observability, revealing substantive realism beyond standard task framing.

proposals.name: Composable Mechanistic Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when multiple components have explicit roles and interfaces that jointly resolve a stated failure mode; score 0 when components are merely concatenated without a reasoned interaction.
proposals.rationale: R09, R13, and R24 describe mobility-navigation, motif-generation, or flow-composition interactions whose value depends on how parts work together.

proposals.name: Extrapolation-Oriented Representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or algorithm is designed to support principled behavior on unseen entities, goals, resolutions, or distributions; score 0 when it is confined to the training configuration.
proposals.rationale: R31, R33, R41, and R57 explicitly construct representations for new subtasks, entities, mesh resolutions, or goals, a transferable quality not captured by benchmark breadth alone.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-Guided Decisions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is estimated and directly determines trust, conservatism, sampling, or action; score 0 when uncertainty is absent or reported only descriptively.
proposals.rationale: R19, R40, and R45 use epistemic uncertainty, out-of-distribution detection, or label uncertainty as active parts of the method’s reasoning.

proposals.name: Causal Diagnostic Decomposition
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the study isolates which components or mechanisms cause observed behavior through interventions, ablations, or controlled comparisons; score 0 when it reports only aggregate comparisons.
proposals.rationale: R15, R27, R36, and R42 deconstruct systems or manipulate training and input factors to identify causes, an analytical depth likely visible in the prose.

proposals.name: Capability-Boundary Probing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation is designed to expose precise failure boundaries using adversarial, counterfactual, transfer, or logically diagnostic tests; score 0 when evaluation uses only routine in-distribution testing.
proposals.rationale: R17, R35, R48, and R53 probe context conflicts, implicit logic, physical triggers, and counterfactual shifts rather than relying solely on ordinary datasets.

proposals.name: Constraint-Aware Efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when resource, privacy, latency, memory, or energy constraints are central to the formulation and reflected in the design; score 0 when efficiency is an afterthought or asserted without design consequences.
proposals.rationale: R02, R08, R28, and R37 make memory, quantization, multiplication count, or encrypted computation integral to the contribution.

proposals.name: Reusable Knowledge Interface
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the learned representation or interface can be reused, updated, composed, or controlled across substantially different tasks; score 0 when it serves only one fixed task with no reuse mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R16, R33, R54, and R57 present knowledge fusion, updateable memory, motor primitives, or factorized values as reusable interfaces.

proposals.name: Formal-Operational Tightness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal definitions, assumptions, guarantees, and algorithmic operations correspond tightly to one another; score 0 when theory is decorative, underspecified, or disconnected from the proposed method.
proposals.rationale: R04, R14, R21, and R45 tie formal objects such as interval bounds, function classes, gradient alignment, or label uncertainty to concrete procedures.

proposals.name: Nontrivial Synthesis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when established ideas are combined to overcome a clearly articulated incompatibility or tradeoff; score 0 when the contribution is an unmotivated aggregation of familiar techniques.
proposals.rationale: R06, R24, and R58 combine Schrödinger bridges with adversarial learning, flow matching with discrete bridges, or message passing with anisotropic long-range structure.

proposals.name: Explicit Scope and Tradeoffs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states important limitations, tradeoffs, or validity conditions and explains their implications; score 0 when it presents uniformly positive claims with no boundary conditions or caveats.
proposals.rationale: R11, R17, R35, and R55 discuss dataset bias, factuality-faithfulness tension, failed logical generalization, or assumptions behind risk analysis, signaling unusually careful scholarship.

proposals.name: Promotional superlative density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much language such as “first,” “remarkable,” “significant,” “unprecedented,” or “state-of-the-art” appears? Judge only its extent, not whether any claim is good, correct, or important.
proposals.rationale: A text model may treat emphatic framing as a shortcut unrelated to research merit. Examples include R03, R11, R18, and R34.

proposals.name: Public artifact and project-page cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract mentions released code, data, checkpoints, project pages, supplementary media, or repository URLs? Judge only the extent, not whether the artifacts are useful or credible.
proposals.rationale: Institutional resources and collaboration networks can leave visible release-language fingerprints while also plausibly enabling stronger work, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R01, R24, R36, and R60.

proposals.name: Canonical benchmark familiarity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract names widely recognized benchmark datasets, task suites, or standard evaluation environments? Judge only the extent, not whether the benchmarks are appropriate or informative.
proposals.rationale: Community familiarity can make conventional benchmark references salient to text models without changing the underlying research merit. Examples include R04, R24, R25, and R50.

proposals.name: Citation lineage density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract contains named attributions, literature lineage, or phrases situating the work among prior studies? Judge only the extent, not whether the citations are accurate or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Seniority and scholarly networks may produce denser literature positioning and may also affect genuine research capability, so this is a mixed nuisance. Examples include R08, R09, R27, and R46.

proposals.name: Formal symbolic texture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract uses equations, Greek symbols, asymptotic notation, formal definitions, or theorem-like language? Judge only the extent, not whether the mathematics is correct or meaningful.
proposals.rationale: Formal notation can act as a prestige or technicality cue to a text model while being independent of research merit. Examples include R08, R29, R46, and R54.

proposals.name: Acronym and coined-label load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract introduces acronyms, branded method names, named datasets, or coined component labels? Judge only the extent, not whether the names are memorable or justified.
proposals.rationale: Naming conventions can create recognizability and salience shortcuts without constituting research merit. Examples include R02, R11, R34, and R52.

proposals.name: Application-scope sprawl
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract lists many domains, datasets, modalities, tasks, environments, or downstream applications? Judge only the extent, not whether the breadth is good or substantiated.
proposals.rationale: Long lists of application contexts can signal ambition or coverage to a text model without directly measuring research merit. Examples include R19, R26, R50, and R53.

proposals.name: Exact-result density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract contains exact percentages, numerical gains, metric values, speedups, error figures, or ranked comparisons? Judge only the extent, not whether the numbers are impressive or reliable.
proposals.rationale: Numerical specificity may function as a confidence cue for a text model even when it is not itself research merit. Examples include R03, R11, R25, and R30.

proposals.name: Submission-production artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract shows raw markup, unusual spacing, broken line hyphenation, malformed URLs, encoding artifacts, or inconsistent formatting? Judge only the extent, not whether the presentation is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Editing and submission pipelines can leave visible formatting fingerprints that affect tokenization or perceived polish without changing research merit. Examples include R36, R45, R58, and R24.

proposals.name: Recency and trend-brand markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract uses era-specific model names, rapidly changing technology labels, or current trend vocabulary such as LLM, GPT-4o, LoRA, diffusion, or 3D Gaussian? Judge only the extent, not whether the topic is fashionable or useful.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing leaves textual traces through contemporary technologies and may also provide access to newer tools that affect genuine work, so this is a mixed nuisance. Examples include R13, R18, R55, and R58.

proposals.name: Diagnosis-to-mechanism coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and the proposed design follows directly from that diagnosis, with the causal chain made explicit; score 0 when motivation, method, and claimed benefit are generic or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R01 links model error to uncertainty-weighted conservatism, while R20 links mixed-domain normalization to separate statistics. R37 similarly connects embedding-layer gradients to a targeted freezing intervention.

proposals.name: Structure-matched inductive bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture or representation encodes a specific structure of the target phenomenon—such as geometry, logic, directionality, or dynamics—and explains why; score 0 when it is a generic model with no task-structure rationale.
proposals.rationale: R03 encodes higher-order structure for logical reasoning, R09 derives a finite-element representation from PDE structure, and R52 explicitly models directional long-range interactions.

proposals.name: Controlled isolation of causal contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract describes controlled removals, substitutions, or matched comparisons that isolate why a component matters; score 0 when only the intact system is compared with baselines and no component-level test is stated.
proposals.rationale: R20 isolates normalization choices and clean/adversarial data effects, R37 isolates the embedding layer, and R59 systematically deconstructs diffusion-model components.

proposals.name: Reusable abstraction across contexts
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one central abstraction is explicitly reused across multiple tasks, domains, resolutions, or downstream uses without changing its core meaning; score 0 when the contribution is tied to one narrow setting or reuse is merely asserted.
proposals.rationale: R21 reuses a neural surrogate for wireless rendering and localization, R38 applies one flow formalism to docking and relaxation, and R44 reuses motor primitives for imitation and task control.

proposals.name: Compositional long-horizon structure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a complex capability is represented as interacting reusable units with explicit composition, sequencing, or coordination; score 0 when complexity is handled by a monolithic predictor or a list of modules without an interaction mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R27 composes mobile manipulation and navigation skills, R47 composes user interests from multiple item facets, and R51 learns ordered subtask hierarchies.

proposals.name: Predictive analytical explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis derives a concrete behavioral, scaling, or algorithmic prediction that the abstract then tests or applies; score 0 when mathematics is decorative, non-predictive, or disconnected from the method.
proposals.rationale: R10 constructs a predictive scaling law, R30 derives complexity guarantees under changing gradient bias, and R42 analytically explains edge-of-stability dynamics.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-aware reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty, ambiguity, or competing knowledge sources are explicitly represented, estimated, and used to guide inference, control, or interpretation; score 0 when the abstract assumes a single certain answer despite an identified ambiguity.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses epistemic uncertainty to blend estimates, R06 estimates out-of-distribution uncertainty, and R46 operationalizes label uncertainty. R24 also distinguishes competing forms of knowledge reliability.

proposals.name: Reproducibility specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives concrete reproduction-enabling details—named datasets or tasks, operating regimes, baselines, artifacts, and implementation availability; score 0 when it offers only generic experimental language or a bare code link or promise.
proposals.rationale: R02, R11, R28, and R55 identify concrete tasks, regimes, artifacts, or released resources. This distinguishes substantive reproducibility information from checklist-friendly publicity alone.

proposals.name: Bounded claims and explicit tradeoffs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are tightly scoped to stated assumptions and the abstract explicitly names limitations, failure modes, or tradeoffs; score 0 when it uses sweeping superiority or application promises without conditions.
proposals.rationale: R24 foregrounds the factuality/context-faithfulness tradeoff, R29 characterizes limits outside the training distribution, and R41 openly reports failure on abstract logic. These contrasts matter beside broad claims in R16 and R18.

proposals.name: Evaluation aligned with deployment constraints
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation measures the task objective together with the central real-world constraint—such as memory, latency, energy, privacy, physical validity, or data access; score 0 when it reports a task metric while ignoring the constraint that motivates the work.
proposals.rationale: R05 couples multiplication savings with accuracy, R11 evaluates extreme bit-width regimes, R17 measures encrypted inference efficiency, and R34 incorporates translation latency into its setup.

proposals.name: Intervention-backed interpretability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when internal features are probed and then causally manipulated or behaviorally checked through an intervention tied to the task; score 0 when interpretability consists only of visualizations, correlations, or labels applied after the fact.
proposals.rationale: R40 probes hidden directions and edits them at inference, while R26 identifies and manipulates personality-related neurons. R09 adds a less direct example by relating learned representations to constituent dynamics.

proposals.name: Operationalized hidden variables
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a previously hidden variable, function class, or tradeoff, defines it operationally, and builds the method around it; score 0 when it merely renames a familiar objective without a measurable construct.
proposals.rationale: R36 identifies which covariate function classes should be balanced, R46 defines label uncertainty, and R19 turns representation-space novelty into cluster visitation estimates.

proposals.name: Transfer tests at the generalization boundary
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when transfer is tested under a clearly specified meaningful shift—such as unseen entities, sensors, resolutions, environments, or counterfactuals—and the setup probes the stated generalization claim; score 0 when evidence is confined to the training distribution or shift is only asserted.
proposals.rationale: R09 tests higher-resolution meshes, R39 uses leave-sensor-out settings, R54 uses counterfactually revised data, and R60 updates memory for unseen entities.

proposals.name: Integration that resolves incompatibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when combining existing ingredients requires and receives a principled interface or modification that resolves a stated incompatibility; score 0 when standard components are simply concatenated under a new name.
proposals.rationale: R05 addresses sparsity being destroyed by Winograd transforms, R11 resolves the quantization–LoRA initialization mismatch, and R55 handles fusion across differing model architectures.

proposals.name: Scientifically diagnostic evaluation instruments
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a benchmark or metric defines a precise construct, uses tasks that distinguish it from nearby constructs, and checks validity or limitations; score 0 when it is only a broad task collection or a single unvalidated proxy.
proposals.rationale: R32 defines and validates implicitness as a distinct construct, R35 addresses gold-standard absence and manipulation robustness, while R53 illustrates how broad multimodal coverage can lack equivalent construct validation.

proposals.name: Abstract length and verbosity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much unusually extended prose, elaboration, or clause-heavy explanation is present. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the verbosity is good, rigorous, or important.
proposals.rationale: Length can be learned as a presentation shortcut rather than a quality signal. R15 and R46 are especially elaborated, while R30 is extremely brief.

proposals.name: Mathematical notation density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much formal notation, equations, asymptotic expressions, symbols, or specialized mathematical syntax appears. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the mathematics is correct or valuable.
