proposals.rationale: Notation density is an observable stylistic cue that may trigger field or sophistication associations without establishing quality. R05 and R27 contain dense formal expressions, while R30 uses compact technical notation.

proposals.name: Acronym and method-brand density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how many named methods, acronyms, datasets, benchmarks, or branded components are introduced or repeated. Judge only naming extent; do not judge whether the names represent good methods.
proposals.rationale: Dense branding can act as a memorability or professionalism shortcut while merely describing packaging. R01 uses FLAG and multiple named components, and R46 introduces ProactiveBench alongside several named systems.

proposals.name: Conversion and formatting artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much visible text contains line-break hyphenation, TeX commands, spacing anomalies, malformed links, stray markup, or other extraction artifacts. Judge only artifact extent; do not judge whether the presentation is good.
proposals.rationale: Text-extraction artifacts can influence a text model independently of the research. R04 contains broken hyphenation and R55 contains a malformed repeated URL.

proposals.name: Promotional superlative language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract uses promotional or superlative wording such as remarkable, unprecedented, state-of-the-art, first, vastly, or extraordinary. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the claims are justified.
proposals.rationale: Promotional vocabulary is a rhetorical style feature, not evidence of research quality. R07 uses repeated first and state-of-the-art claims, while R56 uses extraordinary and substantial-margin language.

proposals.name: Fashionable topic vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract relies on currently fashionable topic markers, such as LLMs, agents, diffusion, preference alignment, privacy, or synthetic data. Judge only vocabulary extent; do not judge whether the topic is important.
proposals.rationale: Venue and community fashion can make certain lexical fields more salient to text models; the same attention may also channel resources toward active topics. R09 and R46 foreground LLM-centered framing, while R38 combines preference learning with GPT-4-era terminology.

proposals.name: Editorial polish
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the prose exhibits grammatical fluency, consistent terminology, smooth transitions, and freedom from awkward or visibly unedited phrasing. Judge only editorial polish; do not judge whether the ideas are good.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing can create a readable textual surface without changing the underlying contribution. R02 is highly polished and fluid, whereas R11 contains visibly awkward constructions such as 'has went'.

proposals.name: Resource-scale signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract signals unusually large models, datasets, model panels, compute scale, or extensive infrastructure. Judge only the amount of signaling; do not judge whether the resources produced good research.
proposals.rationale: Institutional resources can leave visible traces through scale claims and can also enable genuine technical advances, making this a sensitivity channel. R15 mentions ImageNet and ResNet-638, while R16 reports 18K questions and evaluations of 28 models.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract lists distinct datasets, tasks, domains, environments, modalities, or physical-world settings. Judge only breadth; do not judge whether the evaluation is convincing.
proposals.rationale: Access to collaborators, data, and deployment settings leaves a breadth fingerprint that can also support real quality, so the channel is mixed. R08 spans varied RL tasks and simulated and real robots, while R45 covers healthcare and human-activity datasets with leave-sensor-out settings.

proposals.name: Literature-positioning density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract contains named prior authors or papers, historical dates, detailed baseline contrasts, or explicit novelty positioning. Judge only positioning extent; do not judge whether the literature claims are accurate.
proposals.rationale: Seniority and research-network access may influence how extensively authors position work, while also plausibly affecting genuine research quality. R11 cites Oh et al. (2016), R17 cites several named lines of work, and R27 cites Mallinar et al. (2022).
